title: Bhai Lalo's bread
hook: at Saidpur he eats the coarse bread of Lalo the carpenter and turns down the rich Malik Bhago's feast

segments.voice: Yesterday, the udasi: Nanak and Mardana walking out of town for years. Your line was go and see. Where did the new route take you? Day thirty-three.

Imagine two invitations arrive on the same night. One is from the richest man in town. There'll be a long table, silver dishes, the important people of the district, and it would do your reputation a lot of good to be seen there. The other is from a carpenter who lives in a small house at the edge of town. He's offering what he has: a few pieces of coarse, heavy bread. Guru Nanak got both invitations, tradition says, in a town called Saidpur, in the Punjab. The rich man was an official named Malik Bhago. The carpenter was named Lalo. And the whole town was watching to see which door the holy man would walk through. Today, the bread he chose.
screen: `TWO INVITATIONS, ONE NIGHT.` → `A RICH OFFICIAL'S FEAST.` → `A CARPENTER'S COARSE BREAD.`

segments.voice: Nanak went to Lalo's. He stayed with the carpenter, sat on his floor and ate his bread, which tradition describes as rough, made from coarse grain. Malik Bhago was offended. He'd laid on a feast for this visitor, and the visitor had gone to a laborer's hut instead. So he sent for Nanak and demanded to know why. The answer, in the way Sikhs tell it, was simple: Lalo's bread is earned by honest work, with his own hands. Your feast, the Guru said, was paid for by squeezing the poor. Tomorrow we'll see the famous, strange thing tradition says happened next. Today, stay with the choice. Here's why it matters so much on this path. Sikhs describe their way of life with three short commitments. Remember God's name. Share what you have. And earn an honest living, which in Punjabi is kirat. Lalo is kirat with sawdust on his hands. He isn't a priest. He isn't rich. He works, he earns, and he shares what he earns with a stranger at his door, and the Guru treats that coarse bread as the finest food in town. It's not just a story. Lalo shows up in the scripture itself. In one of Guru Nanak's hymns, in raga Tilang, the Guru speaks to him by name, O Lalo, as if talking to a friend. So a carpenter from a small town has his name in the Sikh holy book. Sikhs sometimes say it this way: the bread isn't sweet because of what's in it. It's sweet because of how it was earned.
screen: `HE WENT TO THE CARPENTER'S HOUSE.` · `THE FEAST WAS PAID FOR BY THE POOR.` · `KIRAT — AN HONEST LIVING.` · `LALO'S NAME IS IN THE SCRIPTURE.` · then, large: `HONEST BREAD IS SWEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat one plain meal gratefully. Maybe it's the next thing you eat, a slice of toast, a bowl of rice. For now, settle and bring it to mind, or hold it if it's in front of you. Think about whose hands it passed through: the farmer, the driver, the person at the register, maybe you. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own way. If you don't, just let the plainness be enough. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Lalo's bread. The coarse bread of a carpenter, honestly earned, which Guru Nanak chose over a rich man's feast. Today's word.
Your line: honest bread is sweet. Today, when you eat, notice one thing that was earned by honest work, yours or someone else's. Day thirty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning an honest living, as one of the three pillars of daily life alongside remembering God's name and sharing; the story of Bhai Lalo is one of the best known sakhis told to children.

fork.setup: you're a visiting holy man in Saidpur. the richest man in town invites you to a feast. a carpenter offers coarse bread. where do you eat?
options: the feast: it's rude to refuse the powerful.
fork.reveal: Nanak stayed with Lalo. when Malik Bhago demanded why, the answer was that honest bread was worth more than a feast squeezed from the poor.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kirat, honest work; kirat karni, to earn an honest living, is one of the three Sikh pillars.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint who liked simple food.
what it means: bread honestly earned is honored above wealth taken from others; Lalo is kirat in person.
what a scholar hears: a carpenter named in the scripture itself, Tilang, around Ang 722, addressed by the Guru as a friend.

notes: The Lalo/Bhago story is janamsakhi tradition; Bhago's title (Malik) and his role as an official follow common telling. Confirm.
Tilang hymn addressing Lalo ('jaisee mai aavai khasam kee baanee...') located at Ang 722-723; confirm Ang.
The three pillars (naam japna, vand chhakna, kirat karni) are a later formulation of Sikh teaching; presented as how Sikhs describe their way of life. Confirm.
The Guru's answer to Bhago is paraphrased from tradition; tomorrow covers the milk-and-blood episode.
